title: Construction contractor financing
metaDescription: Construction contractors often compare working-capital lines, equipment financing, and SBA-backed options based on job schedules, receivables, surety-bond requirements, and fleet or equipment needs. Review the industry-specific document and fit differences.
summary: The construction-contractors page explains how work-in-process schedules, receivables, bonds, and equipment needs change the financing comparison for contractors and builders.

hero.title: Construction financing usually follows the job schedule, not just the bid amount.
hero.lead: Contractors often compare working-capital lines, equipment financing, term debt, and SBA-backed options. The right starting point usually depends on whether the pressure comes from project cash-flow timing, bonded contract capacity, or a heavy equipment purchase.

quickAnswer.definition: often starts with line-of-credit, equipment-financing, or SBA-backed comparisons, because lenders usually need to understand project cash-flow timing, accounts receivable, work-in-process, bonding requirements, and equipment demands alongside the contractor's financials.

whoItFitsHeading: When this industry page fits best
bestFitHeading: Common financing starting points for construction contractors

bestFitProducts.title: Business lines of credit
bestFitProducts.description: Often part of the first comparison when project cash-flow timing, payroll, materials, or receivables pressure the business between draws and collections.

bestFitProducts.title: Equipment financing
bestFitProducts.description: Often relevant when the request is really about excavators, trucks, trailers, lifts, or other job-critical equipment.

bestFitProducts.title: SBA 7(a) loans
bestFitProducts.description: Worth comparing when the project blends working capital, equipment, refinance, or broader growth needs into one request.

whoItFits.heading: When contractor financing tends to fit
items: Contractors managing payroll and materials before receivables are collected
Builders or trades comparing a monitored working-capital line against a broader term or SBA structure
Firms that need to add or replace revenue-producing equipment tied directly to projects
Companies whose bonded work, backlog, or job schedule changes how the lender reads the cash-flow request

whenItMayNotFit.heading: When this path may not fit as well
items: If the request is really about buying owner-occupied real estate, the real-estate route is usually the better first comparison.
If the company is not operating project-based or trade-contractor work, another industry or use-case page may fit better than this contractor-focused view.

underwritingFocusCards.title: Work in process and backlog
underwritingFocusCards.description: Bonded and project-based contractors often need the lender or surety to understand the work already underway, not just the next project they want to fund.

underwritingFocusCards.title: Receivables and project timing
underwritingFocusCards.description: SBA's working-capital pilot highlights borrowing against accounts receivable and project financing, which matters when labor and materials are funded ahead of collection.

underwritingFocusCards.title: Bonding capacity and contract requirements
underwritingFocusCards.description: Public and private contracts may require bid, performance, or payment bonds, so financing conversations can overlap with bond eligibility and surety documentation.

typicalDocuments.heading: Common contractor-financing document examples
items: Schedule of work in process or backlog support
Accounts receivable or project-billing support showing how jobs convert to cash
Bid, performance, or payment bond information when bonded contracts are part of the work mix
Equipment quotes or fixed-asset details if the request also includes machines, vehicles, or major tools

alternativePathsHeading: Compare these alternatives if the project changes

alternativePaths.title: Business expansion
alternativePaths.description: Use the broader expansion-intent page if the question is really about a new division, location, or scale-up rather than project-by-project contractor working capital.

alternativePaths.title: Owner-occupied real estate
alternativePaths.description: Use the real-estate path if the project is about a yard, warehouse, or other owner-occupied property rather than operating capital or equipment.

alternativePaths.title: Equipment purchase
alternativePaths.description: Use this route if the contractor's real need is financing one machine or vehicle, not the broader job-schedule cash cycle.

sectionDisclosureHtml: Fund44 is not a lender. Construction-financing eligibility, bond participation, lender availability, collateral requirements, timelines, and terms are determined by third-party lenders, sureties, and program rules. This page is educational only.

commonQuestions.question: What financing paths do construction contractors commonly compare first?
commonQuestions.answer: Lines of credit, equipment financing, SBA-backed options, and term loans are common starting points, depending on whether the need is project cash flow, bonded contract capacity, or a machine or vehicle purchase.

commonQuestions.question: Why does work in process matter for some contractor requests?
commonQuestions.answer: SBA's work-in-process form exists because surety and contractor underwriting often needs to understand the jobs already underway, not just future work. That helps frame backlog, open commitments, and project timing.

commonQuestions.question: Why do surety bonds come up in contractor financing discussions?
commonQuestions.answer: SBA's surety-bond program explains that many public and private contracts require bid, performance, and payment bonds. When bonded work is part of the business mix, bond capacity can overlap with financing and document preparation.

commonQuestions.question: Does Fund44 lend directly to contractors?
commonQuestions.answer: No. Fund44 does not lend directly to contractors. Third-party lenders and, where relevant, sureties determine eligibility, structure, and terms.
